newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: OLYMPICS-BUENOS AIRES TRUMPETS SAFE IMAGE.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-BUENOS AIRES TRUMPETS SAFE IMAGE.

text.p: Buenos Aires is pinning its hopes for the 2004 Olympics on irresistible Latin charm and a reputation as a mecca for lovers of sports ranging from soccer to polo.

The Argentine capital, a noisy city of 12 million on the banks of the mud-brown River Plate, seduces most travellers who venture this far south with its blend of European sophistication and home-grown attractions such as the prime beef and sultry tango.

"Abroad they are falling in love more and more with our city," says Francisco Mayorga, the ex-racing driver heading its Olympic bid, demonstrating the lack of modesty characteristic of the "portenos", as the denizens of the portside city are known.
Vanity aside, Buenos Aires is touting itself as a "safe" option for the Games, especially when compared to its Latin American rival in the contest for 2004, Rio de Janeiro.
It has surprisingly little street crime for its size and athletes and spectators need have little worry about wandering the streets at any time of day or night.
"It's one of the biggest, safest cities in the world," says Mayorga in another burst of porteno pride.

But Buenos Aires has suffered two major guerrilla attacks in recent years against its large Jewish community, bombs in 1992 and 1994 which killed more than 100 people. Argentine police have still not tracked down those responsible.

Security, especially against this kind of fundamentalist violence, has been a major concern for the Olympic organisers since Arab guerrillas killed 11 Israeli athletes at the 1972 Munich Games. But the Argentine Olympic bid committee insists the anti-Jewish bombings were isolated events "in a country without social or racial conflicts."

As well as counting on its image as a sports-loving city with a reputation for soccer, tennis and polo, Buenos Aires makes a historical claim as the only one of the 12 founding nations of International Olympic Committee in 1894 not to have hosted the Games. It is making its fifth bid, after failing in 1936, 1944, 1956, when it was runner-up, and 1968.
The bid has the fanatical support of President Carlos Menem, himself a keen golfer, soccer player and racing driver.
The highlight of Buenos Aires's technical bid is the high density of existing sports facilities near the city centre.

It would stage 90 percent of competitions in a "loop" 14 km long and two km wide along the river between the stadiums of local soccer rivals Boca Juniors, current club of Diego Maradona, and River Plate, site of the 1978 World Cup.

The "Olympic loop" around the city centre already includes a horse-track, fields that host the world's best polo, the Buenos Aires Lawn Tennis Club and the vast Luna Park indoor stadium for boxing events.
River Plate as the Olympic stadium would host athletics, swimming, diving and water polo. Only baseball, badminton and rowing would be held outside the city centre.
Probably the biggest challenge for Buenos Aires' bid, which needs an estimated investment of $551 million, will be the need to boost hotel space by between 50 to 70 percent.
